summary: The IM6 is the SUV half of the IM sub-brand that MG Australia sells through its own dealers as 'IM presented by MG' — a 4.9-metre, 2.3-tonne electric crossover whose specification-per-dollar Australian reviewers consistently call extraordinary, with 800V charging, air suspension and four-wheel steering at XPeng G6 and Zeekr 7X money. The consensus splits sharply on whether it drives like the money: CarExpert and the NRMA rate the cabin, comfort and equipment highly, while Chasing Cars scored the Performance 5.5/10 for a lumpy air-sprung ride, disconnected steering and intrusive driver aids. Reviewers converge again on ownership: real-world consumption of 22-27kWh/100km against WLTP claims, a five-year unconditional warranty well short of the MG-badged cars, and no Australian resale history yet.
pros: 800V architecture on Platinum and Performance takes up to 396kW DC for a claimed 30-80 per cent in 15.2 minutes — roughly triple the peak rate of a Tesla Model Y or XPeng G6; the 400V Premium is capped at 153kW and about 20 minutes
665L boot and 1640L folded on Premium and Platinum (646L/1621L on the Performance) plus a 32L frunk, comfortably ahead of the XPeng G6's 571L and the Zeekr 7X's 539L
The Performance's 572kW/802Nm dual-motor drivetrain claims 0-100km/h in 3.4 seconds at $77,990 drive-away, undercutting a Tesla Model Y Performance by roughly $17,000

Rear-axle steering with up to 12 degrees of angle gives a 10.18m turning circle, and Advanced Air Suspension with continuous damping is standard on the Performance and a $4,990 factory option on Premium and Platinum
Warranty extends to 7 years/unlimited km if every scheduled service is completed inside MG's dealer network, and the high-voltage battery is covered 8 years/160,000km however the car is serviced
cons: IM does not get MG's headline 10-year warranty: the unconditional term is 5 years/unlimited km (7 only with in-network servicing), behind the 7 years on MG's own cars, Kia and Chery, and the NRMA notes not every MG dealer is set up to service IM

Thirsty even on paper: the Performance's declared WLTP consumption is 23.4kWh/100km, against roughly 17.5kWh for a Zeekr 7X Performance and 14.5kWh for a Tesla Model Y Performance, and testers did worse again — CarExpert averaged 24.1kWh/100km and carsales 27kWh/100km, putting realistic touring range nearer 400km than the claimed 505km
Chasing Cars scored the Performance 5.5/10, describing the air-sprung ride as 'knobbly or lumpy' over ordinary urban surfaces and the steering as short on feedback despite the hardware
Rear vision is poor enough that CarExpert calls the mirror setup 'one of the worst', and the driver-assist warnings reset to on at every restart with no explanation of what triggered them

Ownership risk is unpriced: no spare tyre, servicing every 12 months/20,000km averaging $585.80 across the first five visits, and a brand with no Australian resale record that has already cut Platinum and Performance by $2,000-$3,000 each inside 12 months and is running $3,000 cashback on top
